name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Democrats re-introduce nine bills blocked by Hall and vetoed by Whitmer
description: Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July.  The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were […]
text:
Michigan House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said he was "skeptical" of the willingness of House Republican leadership to move forward with the progress of the nine bills, but that Democrats would re-introduce the bills as many times as necessary. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July. 
The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were never transmitted to Whitmer’s desk for her signature prior to the end of that legislative session, and House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) refused to do so once he took control of the chamber at the start of 2025. That led to an 18-month legal battle between the leaders in both chambers, which culminated in the Supreme Court declining to take up the case, leaving a Court of Appeals decision in place that ruled it was unconstitutional for Hall not to transmit the bills to the governor’s desk.
Hours after the Supreme Court’s decision, Whitmer vetoed the bills, a decision that legislators and labor leaders alike called a betrayal. 
Now, legislators are bringing the bills back up, though they face an uphill battle in the Republican-controlled House. Hall’s refusal to transmit the initial versions of the bills leads most to expect that he will not push the legislation through his chamber while he remains at its helm.
House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said that, while he hopes to get these bills passed in the last five months of the current legislative session by “holding Republicans’ feet to the fire in the House,” he would join legislators in re-introducing the bills as many times as needed to — including next session, when Democrats hope to reclaim control of the House — in order to get them passed.
“I have not had conversations with the House Republicans on this, but the offer stands that we are willing to work in good faith to get this done,” Puri said. “I’m skeptical if that’s really going to happen in this year. But you know, the alternative to that is making sure that they don’t need to be a part of the equation in 2027.”
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) is surrounded by Democratic senators and representatives, as well as labor leaders, to announce the re-introduction of the nine bills that were the subject of a state court case and led to a veto from Gov. Whitmer. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren), who was one of the most vocal critics in the legislature of Whitmer’s decision to veto the bills, said she believes some rank-and-file House Republicans want to see these bills passed, and hopes that party leadership will be willing to work with them. 
“Anything is possible. We are all up for re-election,” Xiong said. “Certainly I look forward to hearing their response because now the ball is in their court, and if they want to take their ball home and not play, then they’re not doing the job that they were elected to do. That sends a very clear message to Michigan families.”
At a press conference on Wednesday morning, legislative Democrats were more focused on Hall’s role in keeping the bills from being passed, rather than Whitmer’s. 
Xiong noted that she hopes Whitmer will be willing to work with legislators on updated versions of the legislation. 
When asked if she believed that Whitmer would sign the bills, should they come to her desk, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said that she had been confident in the past and could not speculate on the Governor’s intentions. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“At this point, she is requesting those bills to come to her desk, and as we are introducing them today, we will make the necessary changes so that they meet the muster,” Brinks said. “We believe that they merit her signature. But that ultimately, as we all know, is a decision that she must make.”
A spokesperson for Whitmer’s office said in response to a question about whether or not she would sign the bills, should they make it to her desk again, “As the governor said, she stands ready to work with the legislature to consider new versions.”
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the frontrunner for the Democrats in the 2026 gubernatorial election, said in a press release following Whitmer’s veto that she would sign the bills into law if elected.
The importance of the bills, which include a shield for working families against debt collection practices that seize tax returns made possible by the Earned Income Tax Credit and a measure preventing massive healthcare costs for teachers and school employees, first responders, nurses and other public servants, was emphasized throughout the press conference. 
“For too long, the people of Michigan, the people who make Michigan run, the people who keep our children safe and educated, our communities healthy, and our state moving have been left to shoulder the burden of rising costs and economic uncertainty alone,” Michigan AFL-CIO President Ron Bieber said. “Michigan’s labor movement is committed to doing whatever is necessary to pass the bills reintroduced today by our friends in the House and Senate, these aren’t just pieces of legislation. These are lifelines for working families.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: These Louisiana K-12 school jobs won’t come with a state stipend this year
description: Gov. Jeff Landry’s plan to provide another round of temporary pay stipends to public school employees could exclude thousands of positions that previously received the pay bump.
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry's plan for another round of public school staff stipends from the state has excluded thousands of workers who received them last year. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Gov. Jeff Landry’s plan to provide another round of temporary pay stipends to public school employees could exclude thousands of positions that previously received the pay bump. 
School nurses, therapists and counselors are among the 12,200 positions that qualified for a state pay stipend last year but don’t meet the criteria this school year, according to information the Louisiana Department of Education provided. These exclusions include jobs at charter and traditional public schools.

For the past three school years, the governor and state lawmakers devoted around $200 million annually to pay $2,000 stipends for teachers and $1,000 for school support staff. In 2025, the stipends raised the compensation for more than 101,000 school jobs, according to the state education department. 

But for the 2026-27 school year, Landry and legislators set aside $168 million for stipends — $32 million less than previous years. The reduction has required the state to shed thousands of positions from the stipend-eligible employee list. 
The education department does not yet know the number of stipend recipients from last year who are ineligible this year. School districts haven’t submitted their staffing plans to the state yet, education department spokesman Ted Beasley said in an email last week.
The number of positions from last year that would not have qualified for stipend funding this year provides insight into how many actual employees could face a state pay cut. 
In early June, Landry said the people losing stipends would generally be school administrators who already have much higher salaries than teachers. 

“If you make $50,000 a year, you need a raise a lot more than somebody who makes $160,000,” Landry said last month at the public announcement of his stipend proposal.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Tuesday, the governor’s office said the public’s focus should mostly be on Landry’s advocacy for teachers receiving raises, though the stipends are not permanent pay increases. They maintain the state’s contribution to teacher pay at previous levels. 

“The story that should be written is that Governor Landry has fought tirelessly to deliver pay raises to teachers,” Landry’s spokeswoman Kate Kelly said in a text message Tuesday. “Even when the deck was stacked against him, he continued fighting and is now delivering on that promise.”

Many of last year’s positions that would lose stipend eligibility are administrative jobs. They include almost 3,600 principals, assistant principals and other school-based administrators. They also encompass almost 2,100 central office workers for school districts, according to the state education department. 

Other positions that won’t come with stipends this school year include professionals who typically spend time with students. 

Around 5,550 school therapists, counselors and other specialist positions could see their stipend eligibility eliminated. More than 900 school school nurse jobs could also see the state pay taken away, according to information provided by the state education department. 

The Louisiana Association of Educators, one of the state’s largest teachers unions, represents some of the school workers at risk of losing the state stipend. President D’Shay Oaks said her organization is hearing mostly from school counselors worried about a pay cut. 

“They are not very happy. Some of the parishes are going to find local money and tax-based money to work with them,” Oaks said.  
David Claxton, executive director of the Louisiana Association of School Superintendents and Administrators, agreed with Oaks. He said local districts would try to find a way to backfill the stipend for staff members no longer eligible for them. 

“They will pretty much take care of the others if they can afford it,” Claxton said. 

Landry’s stipend plan is designed to incentivize local governments to take more responsibility for funding teachers and other school employee salaries. 
K-12 districts that provide a raise or temporary stipend paid with local tax money will be able to avoid a cut to their state funding under Landry’s plan. Those that don’t raise pay locally will have to provide stipends using their state funding that would normally go to cover costs such as insurance and building maintenance. 
The governor and lawmakers had hoped voters would approve a state constitutional amendment in May to free up money to replace the existing stipends with a permanent raise. When voters rejected that plan, state officials pivoted to mandating that school districts provide stipends with existing state funds to avoid pay cuts.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Families should not be left wondering’ – School clothing allowance program out of funds in 7 days
description: West Virginia's school clothing assistance program isn’t accepting anymore applications due to running out of funds, according to the state Bureau of Family Assistance. The application window was open for a total of seven days.
text:
(Stock photo by Thanasis/Getty Images)West Virginia’s school clothing assistance program isn’t accepting anymore applications due to running out of funds, according to the state Bureau of Family Assistance. The application window was open for a total of seven days.
The program provides eligible families vouchers to shop for shirts, pants, shoes, coats and more before school starts. In the past, more than 80,000 children statewide have used the clothing allowance.
The program launched later than expected on July 20 while Gov. Patrick Morrisey reviewed the use of federal anti-poverty funds the state uses to pay for the school clothing allowance program.  
The West Virginia Bureau for Family Assistance posted online that, “The 2026 School Clothing Allowance application period has closed effective 11:59 on July 27, 2026, since program funding has been exhausted.”
Earlier this year, lawmakers approved $177 million in Temporary Assistance for Needy Family funding for the state Dept. of Human Services to spend this current fiscal year on programs, including the school clothing allowance program.
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell
“We appropriated the funding requested by the governor for the school clothing allowance from TANF funds, so it is difficult to understand why families experienced weeks of delays only to see the program close after one week,” said Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, who chairs the House Health Committee.
“This program exists to help children prepare for the school year, and families should not be left wondering why promised assistance from the federal government is no longer available. The Bureau for Family Assistance owes the public a clear accounting of how the funds were spent, why the program closed after one week and whether additional eligible families will have an opportunity to receive the benefit,” Worrell said. 
DoHS previously said that clothing allowance applications would be accepted until Aug. 15, or until the available funds are fully allocated, whichever occurs first. 
The department did not respond to an inquiry by time of publishing about how many children successfully applied for the allowance during the last 7 days while the program was open. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha
“The delayed voucher funds after only a week tells us that West Virginia families are struggling more than ever to make ends meet. Children deserve dignity at school, and I hope the administration will work with the Legislature to ensure all children are fed and clothed in our state,” said Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha.
Morrisey has been reviewing TANF funding after saying that the program faced a $43 million structural deficit due to increased COVID-era spending by DoHS. The governor’s administration has not yet publicly shared budget documents that could provide additional details about the deficit. 
Lawmakers based their TANF approval amount earlier this year on Morrisey’s budget request. During the budget process, DoHS officials never alerted lawmakers that the state could face a deficit in TANF funds, which also fund foster care services, Legal Aid, family support centers and more. 
DoHS announced on July 16 that the department was nearing completion of the review of TANF dollars. 
“Today, West Virginia receives approximately $98.8 million in federal dollars each year to support TANF-funded state activities but spends approximately $137 million annually on TANF programs,” DoHS said in a news release. “The difference has been covered using TANF reserve funds – essentially savings accumulated over previous years. At the current expenditure rate, those reserve funds will be exhausted in about 13 months.”
The statement continued, “Those reserve funds help these programs respond when demand unexpectedly increases – whether because more families qualify for assistance or an emergency creates greater need. Spending them down to zero would leave West Virginia without that cushion when families need it most.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Funding gap leaves NJ’s new mental health crisis centers in limbo
description: New Jersey wants to open five mental health crisis centers, including two that are ready to operate. It needs $29 million more to do so.
text:
The state-run crisis response center in Essex County is located within University Behavioral Health Care in Newark. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)State government officials in the spring celebrated the pending opening of two crisis response centers, places where adults in a mental health emergency can get counseling, medication, and be linked with long-term treatment while decompressing for up to 24 hours.
But a lack of funding means the sites, in Essex and Bergen counties, have yet to welcome patients, and it’s not clear when they will.
A timeline for three other crisis centers initially scheduled to open this summer in Camden, Monmouth, and Morris counties also remains a mystery.
Brigitte Johnson is president and CEO of Care Plus NJ, the mental health organization behind the Bergen County location in Paramus.
“We’re stuck in limbo. That’s the most frustrating thing,” Johnson said. “Other states have solved this issue and come up with levels of sustainability. So we need that kind of effort, and I can’t say that it’s not happening, but it’s been a long process.”
The drop-in centers are the third and final element in the 988-crisis response system the state has developed since the three-digit crisis hotline was established nationwide in July 2022. The hotline is aimed at people considering suicide, struggling with addiction, or otherwise dealing with mental health issues.
Since it launched, calls to the hotline have tripled in New Jersey to more than 180,000 annually, and state officials expect to log more than 240,000 requests for help this year, according to the state Department of Human Services, which oversees the program.
The state also created mobile response teams in all 21 counties that can visit callers in person to help triage psychiatric or substance-related crises, groups that were dispatched more than 1,300 times since March 2025, the department said.
In 2024, the department launched the final part of the 988 system, issuing $37 million in grants to five mental health organizations, including Care Plus, to create the crisis centers. The centers are supposed to operate 24/7 and accept drop-in visitors, referrals from other organizations, and people transported there by police. Treatment will be available regardless of someone’s ability to pay.
“How do you create a system but leave the most important part of it out? You know you need a place for people to go. And we have it, and we’re ready to open a door, but we need the funding,” Amie Del Sordo, Care Plus executive senior vice president for crisis and community services, told the New Jersey Monitor.
Care Plus has invested $1 million of its own funds in the project, Del Sordo said, and the state still owes it money for costs accrued in the last fiscal year, in addition to funding to open the doors. The organization renovated the back half of its Paramus headquarters, displacing several existing programs, and has hired a leadership team and medical director, but paused recruiting for other positions until the funding is settled, she said.
The $60.7 billion state budget Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed in late June includes almost $29 million for the suite of crisis response programs, which is slated to cost some $71.4 million in total over the next 12 months, according to a non-partisan legislative analysis. With the state money allocated for the hotline and mobile response and a sharp decline in the federal grants used to build the system, the analysis shows New Jersey needs an additional $29 million-plus to open and operate all five centers this year.
Sen. Joe Vitale (Hal Brown for New Jersey Monitor)
“The centers will literally save lives — that’s not an exaggeration — from the initial 988 call to the emergency mobile response to the crisis centers. All three elements complete the continuum. Anything less is a mistake,” state Sen. Joe Vitale (D-Middlesex) told the New Jersey Monitor.
Vitale, the chair of the Senate health committee, has outlined plans for legislation requiring the state to find $35 million to open the centers this year, after lawmakers’ efforts to add the program into the current budget fell flat. He is also championing a bill that would create a sustainable funding source for the entire 988 system by adding a 40-cent fee to all telephone lines, something done in multiple other states, but the bill has largely stalled.
“The center also must be added as a permanent budget line going forward. They are too critical to have to negotiate their priority every year,” Vitale said.
Maggie Garbarino, a spokesperson for Sherrill, said the administration remains committed to providing “robust mental health services and supports,” including through the 988 system. She declined to say if or how the work would be funded.
“Looking ahead, and especially as federal funding available for this work changes, the Administration is looking at all options to sustain and grow the network of tools for individuals and families in crisis to call for risk-appropriate response and quality behavioral healthcare,” she told the New Jersey Monitor in an email.
Eva Loayza-McBride, spokeswoman for the human services department, said officials there are also committed to identifying funding for the “critical” third and final component of the crisis response system. The agency also supports crisis diversion homes, short-term residential facilities launched in 2024 in Warren, Mercer, and Gloucester counties, she said.
Human Services Commissioner Stephen Cha speaks at the ceremonial ribbon cutting for a new mental health center in Newark on March 31, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Department of Human Services)
Stephen Cha, the human services commissioner, joined leaders from University Hospital and Rutgers Health’s University Behavioral Health Care group in late March to cut a ribbon in the Essex County crisis center, which shares space with UBHC on a Newark campus that includes the hospital and Rutgers New Jersey Medical School facilities.
The space is equipped with lounge chairs, tables, and private screening rooms where people in crisis can talk to clinical experts and peer-support professionals. It is also stocked with medications to treat mental health issues, addiction, and common physical health concerns like diabetes and high blood pressure.
Jennifer Hughes, CEO of NAMI NJ, an advocacy organization for mental health services, said the chaos of an emergency room can exacerbate a person’s symptoms, while crisis centers are designed to have a more calming effect.
“It’s important to really understand what the person’s going through, what they’re feeling, what they’re doing, and having that person-centered care,” Hughes told the New Jersey Monitor, adding, “When someone’s in crisis and they end up in an emergency room, it’s because there’s nowhere else to go.”
More than 700 people died by suicide in New Jersey last year, an increase from 2024, according to state data, and more than 80,000 were screened for serious psychiatric issues. More than 13% of adults here said they were depressed in 2025, according to America’s Health Rankings data for New Jersey.
Del Sordo, with Care Plus, said she regularly gets requests from people who need help, recalling an email she received Thursday with a subject line “urgent.” A family had a loved one who was spiraling, but they worried about taking the person to the emergency room.
She said they were able to get help for that person, but if one of the crisis centers had been open, “they could have walked right in.”
“These are situations that are happening daily, where folks are left to turn to an ER,” she said.
Carolyn Beauchamp, president and CEO of the Mental Health Association in New Jersey, a statewide advocate and service coordinator, said without the crisis centers, we are once again treating mental illness as a “stepchild” to other medical concerns.
“Without them, hospitals will continue to be repositories for those needing mental health care that most hospitals are unequipped or poorly equipped to provide. This means the ill suffer destructive waits, unnecessary trauma and inadequate care,” Beauchamp told the New Jersey Monitor.

title: GOP leaders say the NC budget offers ‘historic’ raises. A top education panel says it’s not enough.
description: Just weeks after the North Carolina General Assembly passed a $34 billion state budget that included 8% average raises for teachers over two years, the state’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education said it’s not enough. The bipartisan panel, assembled in March by Democratic N.C. Gov. Josh Stein, Senate President Pro Tem Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, […]
text:
Thousands of N.C. teachers rallied on May 1, 2026 outside the legislature to say their pay has not kept up with rising inflation or healthcare costs. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Just weeks after the North Carolina General Assembly passed a $34 billion state budget that included 8% average raises for teachers over two years, the state’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education said it’s not enough.
The bipartisan panel, assembled in March by Democratic N.C. Gov. Josh Stein, Senate President Pro Tem Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, and House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, has been working on recommendations to improve teacher training, student advancement, and administrative operations.
Bipartisan education panel unites NC Gov Stein, Republican leaders amid budget rift

At Monday’s meeting, the commission devoted much of its discussion to strengthening the state’s teacher pipeline and its compensation schedule.
“Very simply, we need to pay our teachers more,” said state Superintendent Mo Green during Monday’s commission meeting.
Hall said the new budget offers “historic raises” for teachers, though the largest percentage gains heavily favor early-career educators. Veteran teachers’ salaries have remained relatively stagnant over the past few budget cycles.
Green said teachers at all levels of experience need to be paid more for the state to become the top state for educators in the Southeast.
According to the N.C. Department of Public Instruction, more than 9,100 teachers decided to leave the state’s public schools in 2024-25. That represents a little more than 10% of the public school teachers employed statewide. Beginning teachers left at a much higher rate of 14.7%.
Lisa Godwin, a former North Carolina Teacher of the Year, told her fellow commission members the state should revisit retention bonuses for each year of service. Currently, teachers with 15 to 24 years’ experience don’t get an annual raise for nearly a decade.
“I’m one of those [whose salary] is frozen,” said Godwin, a beginning teacher coach and mentor coordinator for Pender County Schools.
Godwin said North Carolina did not face a perennial teacher shortage in the past.
“See what worked and what was good in the heyday of teaching and education. And let’s bring these things back,” Godwin said.
Brenda Berg, president & CEO of BEST NC, criticized the state budget for eliminating recurring funding for TeachNC, an online platform used to recruit teachers and teacher candidates.
“Teach NC recruited 3,700 candidates last year to educator preparation programs,” Berg said, “which was a 20% increase in EPP enrollment.”
Berg said the commission should recommend that the program be fully funded in the next budget.
Edgecombe Early College High School Principal Matt Bristow-Smith said the panel should consider recommending the indexing  of teacher salaries to inflation to help them keep up with the cost of living.
“What we’ve effectively done is we have lowered the quality of living for teachers because the earning power of what teachers actually make is less than it was a decade ago,” said Bristow-Smith.
House Bill 1178, which proposed indexing teacher salaries starting in 2033-34, didn’t get a hearing in the short session.
Dr. Robert Taylor, superintendent of the Wake County Public School System, summed up what many on the commission were thinking.
“There just needs to be an acknowledgement that if we are going to address teacher compensation, that it’s going to cost us to fix the problem that has been built over the last several years,” said Taylor. “The longer we take to fix it, the harder the problem becomes to fix.”
The Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education did not take a vote at Monday’s meeting. The bipartisan group, which is also discussing recommendations to strengthen literacy and modernize accountability, meets again August 31, 2026.

text:
Left-handed Gov. Dan McKee signs the fiscal 2027 budget at Children's Friend in Providence on Friday, June 12, 2026. In center background looking on is Senate President Valarie Lawson. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)A dual-language public charter school blocked from opening in Providence next fall under a moratorium passed by the General Assembly and signed into law by Gov. Dan McKee filed a lawsuit in federal court Monday.
De La Comunidad Bilingual Public Charter School had moved partially, but not entirely, through the necessary approval pipeline when the state legislature OK’d a three-year moratorium on new charter school approvals, effectively preventing it from opening. McKee, who is seeking reelection, signed the teachers union-backed legislation into law on June 18 over the objections of charter school advocates.
“This law was aimed at one school: ours,” Carol Aguasvivas, board chair of De La Comunidad, said in a statement Monday. “Families chose us. Our community fought for us. And when lawmakers tried to shut the door before we even opened it, we had a responsibility to fight back.”
De La Comunidad planned to serve students from Providence, Pawtucket and Cranston, starting with around 140 students in its first year after opening in the fall of 2027and expanding over time.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Monday, names McKee, House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski, Senate President Valarie Lawson, and the state’s Council on Elementary and Secondary Education as defendants. 
McKee signs charter school moratorium bills with five days to spare, ending uncertainty

Former Providence Mayor Angel Taveras, who is representing the charter school, wrote in the complaint that the charter school ban was a targeted effort. Taveras noted that the original draft of the charter bill was amended to preserve the expansion of another potentially affected charter school, The Greene School, but that the legislature did not “carve out an exception” for De La Comunidad and shot down further amendments.
“The General Assembly purports to want to address the fiscal impacts on school districts associated with students in the districts attending charter schools,” Taveras argued in the suit. “In truth, the Moratorium Bill was targeted to stop De La Comunidad and strip De La Comunidad of its right to obtain approval to operate.”
The complaint is asking the federal court to nullify the moratorium’s effect on De La Comunidad, alleging that the moratorium constitutes “an unconstitutional impairment of contract and a violation of substantive due process.” It also claims that the moratorium’s impact on De La Comunidad skirts both federal and state laws.
The school received preliminary approval to open from the Council on Elementary and Secondary Education on Jan. 5, with state education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green having recommended passage. 
Under Rhode Island Department of Education regulations, a preliminary approval does not guarantee a charter school will receive the charter it needs to open. Applicants still need to complete certain financial, governance, enrollment, staffing and facilities requirements.
The suit argues that De La Comunidad’s preliminary approval — even if downplayed by the General Assembly in its passage of the charter bill — created enforceable rights. The unopened school relied on the K-12 council’s tentative approval with the tacit understanding, the lawsuit argues, that a “school is given final approval to operate” once it satisfies the council’s outline conditions. 
“[T]he activity approved was lawful and permitted at the time of approval, and the conditions in the preliminary charter were, on their face, an invitation to perform,” the lawsuit argues. 
De La Comunidad had completed most of these conditions, according to the suit. The school incorporated, secured federal nonprofit status, developed financial and staffing plans, identified a possible building to operate from and obtained nearly $1.8 million in combined, conditional funding from a Charter School Program Grant, the New School Venture Fund, the Charter School Growth Fund, and the Rhode Island Education Collective.
The Rhode Island Senate voting board is shown during a vote on an amendment to the charter school moratorium bill on June 11, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Broader argument over school funding
The legal contest hinges largely on what rights, if any, the preliminary approval created.
The value of that tentative affirmation also played into the General Assembly’s passage of the bill, which was underscored by a wider debate about how Rhode Island pays for public charter schools versus traditional district schools.
The law blocks new charter approvals for the 2026-2027, 2027-2028 and 2028-2029 school years and also reduces the statewide charter cap from 35 to 28. The state needs this pause, legislative supporters argued, while Rhode Island reconsiders its school funding formula. 
State and local per-pupil funding generally follows students when they transfer to charter schools, but districts can set aside part of that local contribution to allocate toward a district’s fixed costs — operational expenses that don’t budge easily, like building maintenance, utilities and staffing. 
Defending the bill ahead of its successful passage on June 10, House Education Chair Joseph McNamara said Rhode Island could no longer afford to operate these “two school systems” in tandem.
But the broader argument about funding did not persuade all of McNamara’s colleagues during that floor debate, with some speaking up against the moratorium as specifically exclusionary of De La Comunidad. 
Charter school moratorium passes RI House, awaits clearance from a favorable Senate

Rep. Leonela Felix, a Pawtucket Democrat, argued on the House floor on June 10 that the school would serve primarily students of color, and yet it would be the only school immediately impacted by the moratorium. 
Felix tried to recommit the bill to committee, which would subject it to an additional round of legislative review, but her effort was countered by Majority Leader Katherine Kazarian, who objected and suggested moving on to the bill’s ultimately successful vote. 
A day later, in the opposite chamber on the last night of the legislative session, Senate Minority Leader Jessica de la Cruz proposed an amendment to allow preliminarily approved schools to proceed with the opening process.
“Preliminary approval is just that, it is preliminary,” Sen. Melissa Murray, the bill’s sponsor, said that night, urging her colleagues to reject the minority leader’s amendment. 
The amendment still failed despite drawing 15 votes of support — more than twice the six senators who opposed the moratorium itself.
McKee was ‘Against a Moratorium Before He Was for It’
Still, the Senate had approved an earlier amendment allowing The Greene School, an existing charter school in West Greenwich, to move forward with an expansion approved the same day De La Comunidad received preliminary approval.
That approvals allowed The Greene School to add 168 students, including 112 during the years covered by the moratorium. De La Comunidad would have added 140 students over the three years, and 96 more in the 2029-2030 school year.
The suit characterizes McKee as dealing the final blow against De La Comunidad, despite the fact that, as one heading in the lawsuit puts it, the governor was “Against a Moratorium Before He Was for It.” McKee had expressed support for charter schools in the past.
De la Comunidad leadership “met with Governor McKee to urge him to veto the Moratorium Bill,” the suit recounts, a meeting which McKee also referenced in public comments to reporters after he had signed the moratorium bill. 
“During their meeting, Governor McKee confirmed that De La Comunidad had been specifically targeted by the advocates of the Moratorium Bill,” the complaint reads.
The complaint also focuses on opposition from Rhode Island’s two major teachers unions — the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals (RIFTHP) and the National Education Association Rhode Island, of which Senate President Lawson is also president — as instrumental in pushing the moratorium to victory. 
NEARI spokesperson Stephanie Mandeville said the organization needed time to review the lawsuit before deciding whether it would be able to comment. A representative for the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McKee received an endorsement from the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals on Friday.
McKee backed a charter school moratorium. Now a major teachers union has endorsed him.

McKee’s office is leaving comment on the matter up to the courts.
“Because this is now the subject of litigation, it will be addressed through the courts,” spokesperson Laura Hart said in an email, adding that McKee remained focused on educational access and pointed to school construction spending, academic gains, reduced chronic absenteeism and the addition of 21 after school learning centers planned statewide.
Spokespeople for Blazejewski and Lawson said the legislative leaders had not received the complaint and referred questions to the Attorney General’s Office, which would represent them in the matter.
The AG’s spokesperson, Tim Rondeau, said the office “had not yet been served with the lawsuit, but we will review once we receive it.”
Victor Morente, a spokesperson for the education department, confirmed that the agency is “aware of the lawsuit,” but would stick to its “longstanding practice” of not commenting on pending litigation.
The case has been assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge John J. McConnell Jr.

title: ‘It puts special education back 50 years.’ Ohio advocates concerned over recent federal changes.
description: Ohio special education advocates fear recent changes to the U.S. Department of Education will cause confusion, delays, and a loss of service to students.  The Trump administration announced in June it will move the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Office for Civil […]
text:
Ohio school children in a classroom. (Photo by Morgan Trau.)Ohio special education advocates fear recent changes to the U.S. Department of Education will cause confusion, delays, and a loss of service to students. 
The Trump administration announced in June it will move the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Office for Civil Rights to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The special education office is responsible for making sure states follow the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), a federal law that ensures students with disabilities have access to a free and appropriate public education. 
The civil rights office investigates complaints from students and families.
Dee Marks sits on the Member Organization Council, an arm under the governing board of the Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities.
“For special education in Ohio, it means the process of children with disabilities getting their needs met just got significantly more complicated,” Marks said.
“There’s significant fear that it’s going to degrade the programs and services that have historically been provided under IDEA to the point where students with disabilities will no longer be educated to the level that the law dictates that they should be educated to.” 
About 14% of Ohio students receive special education services, said Jennifer Webb, past president for the Council for Exceptional Children’s Ohio chapter. 
“It puts special education back 50 years to when we were diagnosing and trying to fix kids versus identifying them to give them the services they need to help them learn the best,” said Webb, chair of the teacher education programs at Malone University, a private university in Canton. 
This move also creates a stigma that students with disabilities are viewed as having a medical need first, instead of being viewed as a student first, Marks said. 
For example, she talked about students with disabilities who are blind. 
“You have specialized needs, but all of those needs are focused on education … that student navigating the education building, accessing the curriculum, making sure that it’s in braille or audio so that that student has access,” Marks said. 
She wonders if the focus would now be a medical first model under HHS. 
“It becomes less about them getting access to the education and more focus on that student who’s blind, which then becomes a big concern that that student might be segregated because they’re different,” Marks said. 
Robyn Linscott, director of education and family policy at The Arc of the United States, agrees. 
“Moving IDEA oversight into HHS pushes students with disabilities toward a medical model, where disability is treated as a diagnosis to manage instead of a natural part of human life,” she said in a statement. 
“When that mindset drives education decisions, students are more likely to be segregated, underestimated, or treated as separate from the school community.”
The U.S. Department of Education will continue to be in charge of the statutory responsibilities over special education as required by federal law, but this shifts the day-to-day operations to HHS. 
“It adds another layer of complexity because two departments are involved, and one is still going to have the ultimate responsibility for this other department underneath it, but then how does a parent of a child with a disability who has an issue navigate that?” Marks asked.  
She also wonders how HHS will be able to support students’ educational needs. 
“The Department of Education has, for decades, been in charge of special education, and all of a sudden they just carve special education out, send it to Health and Human Services, and they’re not qualified to handle that programming,” she said. 
This move further shrinks the U.S. Department of Education as President Donald Trump works to fulfill his campaign promise to dismantle the department. 
The Education Department had announced 10 earlier interagency agreements, or IAAs, with HHS, Labor, Interior, State and Treasury, which transfer several of Education’s responsibilities to those agencies.
